newsitem.title: USA: Fat Treasury yields to give dlr/yen limited boost.
newsitem.headline: Fat Treasury yields to give dlr/yen limited boost.

text.p: A recent backup in Treasury bond yields has revived Japanese interest in comparatively lucrative U.S. paper, but will probably trigger only limited dollar/yen gains, analysts said.

With the dollar already seen fully valued by many market players, foreign-based Treasury purchases will most likely be hedged in the foreign exchange markets to guard against losses from dollar/yen backsliding, analysts said.

"Some of this is going to unwind. There will probably be some kind of insurance policy writing as time goes on and exchange rate uncertainty starts to get a little higher," said Sandy Batten, international economist at Citibank.

Japanese individuals, as well as pension funds and life insurers have flocked to U.S. bonds as the spread between the 30-year Treasury yield and that on the 10-year Japanese government bond has ballooned to nearly 500 basis points.
The benchmark 30-year bond now pays 7.09 percent, a whopping 482 basis points over the 10-year JGB.
That spread is the widest since 1985 and far too tempting for yield-starved Japanese players to pass up, analysts said.

"The Japanese, and foreigners in general, are taking a huge amount of Treasury market issues," said Arthur Alexander, president of the Japan Economic Institute of America, a research group partly funded by Japan's Ministry of Finance.
A concurrent rally by the dollar, which reached a 56-month high near 127 yen on Wednesday, facilitates Japanese purchases of Treasuries by enhancing their yield via foreign exchange gains.
But when the dollar stops climbing, or appears ready to surrender some gains, Japanese players will sell it short to protect themselves, pressuring the greenback, analysts said.

"I think they will keep holding Treasuries. They will just sell the dollar in the futures and options markets to hedge their positions, but they won't sell those (bond) positions," said Takanobu Igarashi, senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd.
Many foreign exchange players view the 130-yen level as a near-term limit, with Japanese policy-makers and possibly even their U.S. counterparts seen uncomfortable with much further dollar gains.
Japan's trade surplus with the United States has begun to grow again after several months of shrinkage, which currency players see inevitably pressuring the greenback.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has recently reiterated his position that currencies should not be used as trade policy tools.

But Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara gently admonished dollar bulls on Wednesday, saying Japan could intervene to correct currency moves "... in cases in which rates deviate greatly from economic fundamentals."
"If you were forced to pick, there's a lot less upside potential for dollar/yen than downside potential. But that doesn't mean dollar/yen is going to turn around any day now," said Batten.
Alexander sees a quantifiable relationship between the T-bond/JGB spread and dollar/yen.
For every percentage-point gain in the yield spread, dollar/yen should rise 2.0 percent, according to Alexander's rule-of-thumb.
So as long as the dollar is still playing catch-up to the T-bond, investors need not fear a dollar/yen pullback.
"Until we get this increase (to match the yield) differential, there is a flow of Japanese funds into American investments," Alexander said.
"But you really have to take the possible appreciation of the yen into account. That's when the (dollar) hedging might come in," he added.

Japanese Treasury purchases dwindled over the first quarter of 1997, which corresponds to Japan's fiscal fourth quarter, as institutions completed an annual exercise of repatriating capital for yearend window-dressing purposes, analsyts said.

Igarashi cited MOF data showing Japanese players bought only 0.1 trillion yen ($793 million) worth of U.S. securities in January and February, compared to 2.4 trillion yen ($19.2 billion) in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 1.1 trillion yen ($8.73 billion) in the third quarter.
But Igarashi said he expects the April data, which will be released in late May, to show a resumption of heavy Japanese Treasury buying.
"Japanese investors think the 500-basis-point differential between the bonds of the two countries is very attractive," he said.
(( -- Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664 ))
